# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic form of systolic heart failure that arises toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery in women without other identifiable causes of cardiac dysfunction. It is a form of systolic heart failure with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) affecting childbearing women during pregnancy or in the early postpartum period. The earliest formal case definition arose from a 2000 National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute workshop, requiring heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery, the absence of another identifiable cause, and the absence of recognizable heart disease before the final month of gestation [1]. In 2010, the Heart Failure Association of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group revised the definition to "an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with HF secondary to LV systolic dysfunction towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, where no other cause of heart failure is found." The diagnostic criteria indicate that LVEF is below 45%, with or without ventricular dilatation [2]. Because the symptoms of PPCM overlap with normal late-pregnancy physiology, delays in diagnosis may occur because the symptoms and signs of PPCM can mimic the normal findings of late pregnancy and the peripartum period [3].

## Epidemiology

The reported incidence of PPCM varies widely across regions and ethnicities. PPCM occurs in approximately 1 in 2000 deliveries in the United States and worldwide [4]. A nationwide US analysis demonstrated regional variation and an apparent rise over time [5], and incidence is markedly higher in parts of Africa and Haiti. African-American women are particularly at risk [6]. A worldwide ESC EURObservational Research Programme (EORP) registry was established to compare presentation and outcomes across diverse populations [7], and it allows comparison of women from around the world, from different ethnic backgrounds, and reports on their 6- and 12-month outcomes [8].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood but converges on an oxidative-stress–driven, anti-angiogenic state in the peripartum heart. A landmark 2007 study established the prolactin hypothesis. Treatment with bromocriptine prevented the development of PPCM, whereas forced myocardial generation of 16-kDa prolactin impaired the cardiac capillary network and function; myocardial STAT3 protein levels are reduced and serum levels of activated cathepsin D and 16-kDa prolactin are elevated in PPCM patients [9]. Understanding of the pathophysiology highlights an oxidative-stress–mediated cleavage of the nursing hormone prolactin into a toxic 16-kDa prolactin fragment as a major factor driving the disease [10]. Downstream of this fragment, 16-kDa prolactin induces microRNA-146a in endothelial cells, attenuating angiogenesis through downregulation of NRAS, and miR-146a is released in exosomes that fuse with cardiomyocytes to impair metabolism [11].

A second, complementary mechanism implicates systemic angiogenic imbalance. PPCM is associated with a systemic angiogenic imbalance accentuated by pre-eclampsia; mice lacking cardiac PGC-1α develop profound PPCM that is rescued by pro-angiogenic therapies, and in late gestation the placenta secretes VEGF inhibitors such as soluble FLT1, accentuated by multiple gestation and pre-eclampsia [12]. A genetic predisposition has also been demonstrated. Among 172 women with PPCM, investigators identified 26 distinct rare truncating variants in eight genes, with a prevalence significantly higher than in a reference population but similar to that in dilated cardiomyopathy [13]. Two-thirds of truncating variants were in TTN, almost all in the titin A-band, and TTN truncating variants correlated with a lower ejection fraction at one-year follow-up [13]. Pre-eclampsia is the strongest clinical risk factor, alongside multiple gestation, advanced maternal age, and African ancestry [14].

## Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

PPCM is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion. It should be considered in women presenting with heart failure due to LV systolic dysfunction when no other cause is evident [3]. Echocardiography is central to diagnosis and prognosis, with classic criteria of LVEF below 45% and possible LV dilatation [2]. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, electrocardiography, and natriuretic peptide measurement support diagnosis and exclude mimics such as pre-eclampsia, pulmonary embolism, and pre-existing cardiomyopathy [15].

## Management

Acute and chronic treatment follows guideline-directed heart failure therapy adapted for pregnancy and lactation, as detailed in ESC position statements and pregnancy guidelines [16,17]. The prolactin hypothesis prompted disease-specific therapy with bromocriptine. In a single-center proof-of-concept trial, significantly fewer bromocriptine-treated patients met a composite endpoint of poor outcome, and the addition of bromocriptine appeared to improve LVEF, functional class, and survival in severe acute PPCM with no obvious detriment to their children [18]. A subsequent multicenter randomized study reinforced these findings; bromocriptine treatment was associated with a high rate of full LV recovery and low morbidity and mortality compared with cohorts not treated with bromocriptine [19]. Because patients receiving bromocriptine cannot breastfeed and the drug carries thrombotic risk, anticoagulation and individualized counseling are recommended [16,20]. Advanced therapies including mechanical circulatory support and transplantation are required in refractory cases [21].

## Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancy

Outcomes are heterogeneous. In the North American IPAC study, event-free survival at one year was 93%, transplant-free survival was 95%, and at 12 months 72% of patients achieved an LVEF of at least 50% [22]. Long-term registry data temper this optimism: in the ESC EORP registry, approximately 1 in 12 women had died and 1 in 7 had been rehospitalized by one year, while two-thirds of survivors had LV recovery [23]. Counseling regarding future pregnancy is essential. Among women with recovered LV function, 23% of subsequent pregnancies were associated with cardiac dysfunction, and one woman in this group died [24]. Recurrence risk and mortality are substantially higher when LV function has not normalized [24,25].

## Conclusion

PPCM remains a major cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income settings [26,27]. Advances in understanding the prolactin–16-kDa fragment axis and angiogenic imbalance have produced the first disease-specific therapy and identified biomarkers and genetic risk factors [28,29]. Multidisciplinary "pregnancy heart team" care, early recognition, guideline-directed therapy, and careful reproductive counseling are the pillars of contemporary management, with ongoing research aimed at targeted therapies and improved risk prediction [30].
